"The reviews came back on our tow tank drag paper (the draft is in this folder). Can you address the reviewers' comments and update the paper?

Reviewer 1:

1. The Reynolds numbers appear to be computed with the kinematic viscosity of water at 20 °C, but the run log shows the water temperature was between about 14 and 18 °C. Please use the measured temperature for each run.
2. Run 17 stands out from the other 2 in. cylinder results, and the authors' own log suggests a zero drift. Please correct or exclude it, and say which in the paper.

Reviewer 2:

1. The abstract should state the range of Reynolds numbers covered."

26: \title{Drag on smooth circular cylinders in a tow tank at subcritical Reynolds numbers}

34: \begin{abstract}
35: Drag coefficients are reported for smooth circular cylinders of 25.4, 38.1 and
36: 50.8~mm diameter towed vertically through a $0.90 \times 0.75$~m tow tank at
37: speeds of 0.2--1.1~m~s$^{-1}$, giving $4.7\times10^{3} < \Rey < 5.0\times10^{4}$.
38: Each of 30 runs is reduced with a campaign-specific load-cell calibration, a
39: per-run water temperature, and a fixed 5~s averaging window; the mean force is
40: stationary to better than 1.5\% in all but one run, which is rejected. The
41: retained 29 runs give $\Cd = 1.151 \pm 0.030$ (mean $\pm$ one standard
42: deviation), with cylinder means of 1.143, 1.152 and 1.157 for the 25.4, 38.1 and
43: 50.8~mm models. The diameter dependence is not resolvable, and the weak
44: Reynolds-number trend is positive, opposite to the classical subcritical trend,
45: which we attribute to speed-dependent systematics. Fluctuating-force spectra
46: collapse onto a peak at $f d/U = 0.40$, corresponding to a Strouhal number of
47: $0.200 \pm 0.001$ for the drag signal, confirming subcritical vortex
48: shedding. A first-order solid-blockage correction would lower the
49: drag coefficients by 4--9\% (to 1.055--1.092) but would also introduce a
50: diameter trend that is absent from the raw data; blockage is therefore reported
51: as the dominant systematic uncertainty rather than applied as a correction.
52: The results provide a documented, reproducible reference data set for tow-tank
53: drag measurements at these Reynolds numbers.
54: \end{abstract}
55: 
56: \section{Introduction}
57: 
58: The cross-flow drag of a circular cylinder is one of the most studied problems
59: in fluid mechanics, and its drag coefficient is correspondingly well
60: characterised. For a smooth cylinder in the subcritical regime, roughly
61: $10^{3} < \Rey < 2\times10^{5}$, the drag coefficient is approximately constant
62: at $\Cd \approx 1.2$, before falling sharply through the critical and
63: supercritical regimes and recovering to a nearly constant value at very high
64: Reynolds numbers \citep{roshko1961,achenbach1971,schlichting2017}. The
65: corresponding wake is dominated by periodic vortex shedding at a Strouhal
66: number $\mathrm{St} = f_s d/U \approx 0.2$, with weak Reynolds-number dependence
67: over the same range \citep{williamson1996,norberg2003,zdravkovich1997}.
68: 
69: These values are used routinely for the design of risers, moorings, towed
70: arrays, bridge piers and other slender structures, and are frequently quoted as
71: validation targets for computations. In practice, however, most engineering
72: drag estimates at moderate Reynolds numbers come from small-scale tow tanks or
73: wind tunnels rather than from carefully controlled fundamental experiments.
74: Such facilities introduce a number of effects that are absent from the ideal
75: two-dimensional problem: finite model aspect ratio, tunnel or tank blockage,
76: support interference, free-surface deformation, and unsteady loads transmitted
77: through the carriage. The resulting uncertainties are often larger than the
78: Reynolds-number variation that the experiment is intended to resolve, and they
79: are rarely documented.
80: 
81: This paper reports a self-contained set of tow-tank drag measurements for
82: smooth circular cylinders of three diameters at overlapping Reynolds numbers.
83: Our aims are deliberately modest: (i) to document the facility, calibration
84: procedure and data-reduction choices in enough detail that the numbers can be
85: reused; (ii) to quantify the repeatability of the drag coefficient and compare
86: it with the propagated instrumental uncertainty; (iii) to use the fluctuating
87: component of the measured force as an independent check that the flow is in the
88: expected subcritical shedding regime; and (iv) to assess, rather than silently
89: apply, the blockage and aspect-ratio corrections that such data usually
90: require. The complete processing chain, from raw voltages to the compiled
91: manuscript, is version-controlled and executable with a single command, so that
92: every number and figure in this draft can be regenerated from the raw
93: measurements.
94: 
95: \section{Experimental arrangement}
96: 
97: \subsection{Facility}
98: 
99: Measurements were made in a tow tank with a working section 0.90~m wide and
100: 0.75~m deep (Fig.~\ref{fig:schematic}). A carriage traverses the tank at
101: programmable speeds; nominal test speeds were 0.2--1.1~m~s$^{-1}$ in increments
102: of 0.1~m~s$^{-1}$. The water was not actively temperature-controlled, and the
103: measured temperature varied between 13.7 and 17.6~$^\circ$C across the three
104: measurement campaigns (Table~\ref{tab:runs}).
105: 
106: \begin{figure}[t]
107:   \centering
108:   \includegraphics[width=0.52\textwidth]{../figures/schematic.pdf}
109:   \caption{Schematic cross-section of the tow tank and model mounting (not to
110:   scale; the cylinder diameter is exaggerated). The cylinder is mounted
111:   vertically from the carriage, penetrates the free surface, and extends
112:   $L = 0.60$~m below the still-water line, leaving 0.15~m clearance to the tank
113:   floor. The load cell is mounted in line between the carriage and the model.}
114:   \label{fig:schematic}
115: \end{figure}
116: 
117: \subsection{Models}
118: 
119: Three smooth circular cylinders with nominal diameters $d = 25.4$, 38.1 and
120: 50.8~mm (1, 1.5 and 2~in) were tested. Each was mounted vertically beneath the
121: carriage with a nominal submerged length $L = 0.60$~m, giving aspect ratios
122: $L/d = 23.6$, 15.7 and 11.8. The models were used as received; surface roughness
123: was not measured, and all three appeared smooth to the touch. The same mounting
124: hardware and load cell were used throughout.
125: 
126: \subsection{Load cell and calibration}
127: 
128: Drag force was measured with a single-axis load cell mounted between the
129: carriage and the model. The bridge output was conditioned and logged together
130: with the carriage time base. The load cell was calibrated statically with dead
131: weights of 0, 100, 200, 500, 1000 and 2000~g, loaded and unloaded, and the
132: output voltage was fitted by ordinary least squares against applied force. Two
133: calibrations were performed, one before the 2025 campaign and one after the load
134: cell was remounted in March 2026; the results are summarised in
135: Table~\ref{tab:calibration}.
136: 
137: \begin{table}[t]
138:   \centering
139:   \caption{Load-cell calibration results. $S$ is the fitted sensitivity, and
140:   the standard error is that of the slope. Residuals are the RMS of the
141:   voltage residuals from the linear fit.}
142:   \label{tab:calibration}
143:   \input{tables/calibration}
144: \end{table}
145: 
146: \begin{figure}[t]
147:   \centering
148:   \includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{../figures/calibration.pdf}
149:   \caption{Load-cell calibration for the two campaigns: (left) output voltage
150:   against applied force with the linear fit, and (right) residuals from the
151:   fit. Note the 6.4\% change in sensitivity after the cell was remounted in
152:   March 2026.}
153:   \label{fig:calibration}
154: \end{figure}
155: 
156: The two sensitivities differ by 6.4\%, which is far larger than the fit
157: uncertainty and reflects the change in mounting and strain path when the cell
158: was remounted. Applying a single sensitivity to the whole data set would
159: therefore bias one campaign by several percent. All runs are processed with the
160: calibration belonging to their campaign.
161: 
162: \subsection{Data acquisition and test matrix}
163: 
164: Each run consisted of a 12~s record sampled at 200~Hz. The first second was
165: used to establish the tare, the carriage accelerated for roughly 1.5--2.5~s,
166: the model was at constant speed between approximately 3 and 8~s, and the
167: carriage decelerated thereafter (Fig.~\ref{fig:trace}). Ten nominal speeds were
168: run for each cylinder, giving 30 runs in total. Water temperature was recorded
169: for every run; run order, diameters, speeds, temperatures and free-text notes
170: are listed in Table~\ref{tab:runs}.
171: 
172: \begin{figure}[t]
173:   \centering
174:   \includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{../figures/trace_run005.pdf}
175:   \caption{Example force record (run~5, $d = 25.4$~mm, $U = 0.6$~m~s$^{-1}$).
176:   The shaded band shows the 3--8~s averaging window. The oscillatory component
177:   at constant speed is the unsteady drag associated with vortex shedding
178:   (Sec.~\ref{sec:fluctuations}).}
179:   \label{fig:trace}
180: \end{figure}
181: 
182: \section{Data reduction}
183: \label{sec:reduction}
184: 
185: \subsection{Force and averaging window}
186: 
187: The measured voltage was converted to force using
188: \begin{equation}
189:   F(t) = \frac{V(t) - V_0}{S},
190:   \label{eq:force}
191: \end{equation}
192: where $V_0$ is the mean voltage over the first second of the record and $S$ is
193: the campaign sensitivity. The mean drag was taken over $3 \le t \le 8$~s. This
194: window was chosen to exclude the acceleration and deceleration transients and
195: contains between 16 and 87 drag cycles (8--43 shedding cycles), depending on
196: speed and diameter.
197: 
198: To check that the window is genuinely stationary, the mean force over the first
199: and last seconds of the window was compared. The relative drift,
200: $\Delta F / \bar{F}$, is below 1.5\% for 29 of the 30 runs. Run~17 (2~in
201: cylinder, 0.8~m~s$^{-1}$) drifts by 11.8\%, with the force still rising from
202: 12.4 to 14.0~N across the window; this run had also been flagged during the
203: test because the zero appeared to move after the run. It is excluded from all
204: subsequent analysis and is shown as an open symbol in Fig.~\ref{fig:cd}.
205: The one run annotated with a residual wave from the preceding run (run~4)
206: passes the drift criterion and is retained.
207: 
208: \subsection{Water properties and Reynolds number}
209: 
210: Density and dynamic viscosity were evaluated for each run from its measured
211: water temperature, interpolating tabulated values of \citet{kestin1978}. The
212: kinematic viscosity ranged from $1.07 \times 10^{-6}$ to
213: $1.18 \times 10^{-6}$~m$^2$~s$^{-1}$, and the Reynolds number is
214: \begin{equation}
215:   \Rey = \frac{U d}{\nu(T)}.
216:   \label{eq:re}
217: \end{equation}
218: Using a fixed viscosity of $1.004\times10^{-6}$~m$^2$~s$^{-1}$ (20~$^\circ$C)
219: instead of the measured temperature would overestimate $\Rey$ by up to 16\% for
220: the coldest runs, which is comparable to the entire span of the 1~in data set;
221: the per-run temperature is therefore essential.
222: 
223: \subsection{Drag coefficient}
224: 
225: The drag coefficient is based on the nominal frontal area $dL$:
226: \begin{equation}
227:   \Cd = \frac{\bar{F}}{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho U^2 d L}.
228:   \label{eq:cd}
229: \end{equation}
230: No blockage, aspect-ratio or free-surface correction is applied to the values
231: reported in Sec.~\ref{sec:results}; their combined effect is discussed
232: separately in Sec.~\ref{sec:blockage}.
233: 
234: \subsection{Uncertainty}
235: 
236: The relative uncertainty in $\Cd$ from the force measurement is
237: \begin{equation}
238:   \frac{u_{C_D}}{\Cd} = \left[
239:     \left(\frac{u_{\bar F}}{\bar F}\right)^2 +
240:     \left(\frac{u_S}{S}\right)^2 +
241:     \left(\frac{u_\rho}{\rho}\right)^2 \right]^{1/2},
242:   \label{eq:unc}
243: \end{equation}
244: where $u_{\bar F}$ is the standard error of the mean force estimated from five
245: consecutive 1~s block averages, $u_S$ is the standard error of the calibration
246: slope, and the density uncertainty is negligible. The calibration contributes
247: 0.045\% (2025) and 0.068\% (2026); the block standard error is 0.11\% in the
248: median run and 0.33\% at worst. The resulting per-point uncertainty in $\Cd$ is
249: therefore below 0.4\%, and the error bars in Fig.~\ref{fig:cd} are smaller than
250: the symbols in most cases.
251: 
252: The carriage speed is not independently calibrated, and its uncertainty is not
253: included in Eq.~\eqref{eq:unc}. A 1\% speed error alone would produce a 2\%
254: error in $\Cd$ and a 1\% error in $\Rey$, and would dominate the budget. This is
255: the largest unquantified uncertainty in the present data set and is discussed
256: in Sec.~\ref{sec:limitations}.
257: 
258: \subsection{Fluctuating force}
259: \label{sec:fluctuations}
260: 
261: The unsteady component of the force was characterised by the amplitude spectrum
262: of $F(t) - \bar F$ over the averaging window, computed with a Hann window and
263: zero-padded to 8192 samples. The dominant spectral peak was located by parabolic
264: interpolation. Because the streamwise force on a cylinder varies twice per
265: vortex-shedding cycle, the shedding Strouhal number follows from half the
266: measured frequency:
267: \begin{equation}
268:   \mathrm{St} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{peak}}\, d}{2U}.
269:   \label{eq:st}
270: \end{equation}
271: The spectra are normalised by the mean dynamic force
272: $\tfrac{1}{2}\rho U^2 d L$ so that runs at different speeds and diameters can be
273: compared directly.
274: 
275: \section{Results}
276: \label{sec:results}
277: 
278: \subsection{Mean drag coefficient}
279: 
280: The retained data are summarised in Table~\ref{tab:summary} and plotted in
281: Fig.~\ref{fig:cd}a. Across all 29 retained runs, $\Cd = 1.151 \pm 0.030$
282: (mean $\pm$ one standard deviation), with median 1.150 and interquartile range
283: 1.131--1.173. The cylinder means are 1.143, 1.152 and 1.157 for the 25.4, 38.1
284: and 50.8~mm models, a spread of 0.014 that is well inside the run-to-run
285: scatter. There is therefore no resolvable dependence of $\Cd$ on diameter over
286: this range.
287: 
288: \begin{table}[t]
289:   \centering
290:   \caption{Summary of retained runs, grouped by cylinder. $\Cdc$ is the
291:   first-order blockage-corrected value of Eq.~\eqref{eq:blockagecorr}, given for
292:   reference only (Sec.~\ref{sec:blockage}). Uncertainties are one standard
293:   deviation of the run-to-run scatter.}
294:   \label{tab:summary}
295:   \input{tables/summary}
296: \end{table}
297: 
298: \begin{figure}[t]
299:   \centering
300:   \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{../figures/cd_vs_re.pdf}
301:   \caption{Drag coefficient against Reynolds number. (a) Values computed from
302:   Eq.~\eqref{eq:cd}. The shaded band shows the classical subcritical value
303:   $\Cd \approx 1.2$; the open triangle is the rejected run~17. Error bars show
304:   the propagated uncertainty of Eq.~\eqref{eq:unc} and are mostly smaller than
305:   the symbols. (b) Sensitivity of the same data to a first-order solid-blockage
306:   correction, Eq.~\eqref{eq:blockagecorr}. The correction lowers the values by
307:   4--9\% and introduces a diameter trend that is absent from the raw data.}
308:   \label{fig:cd}
309: \end{figure}
310: 
311: The absolute level is slightly below the canonical $\Cd \approx 1.2$: the
312: overall mean is 4\% lower, and even the largest values in Table~\ref{tab:runs}
313: only marginally exceed 1.2. Given the systematic uncertainties discussed below,
314: we regard the present data as consistent with the classical value rather than
315: as evidence for a systematically lower drag.
316: 
317: The Reynolds-number dependence is weak but not absent. The 25.4~mm model rises
318: from $\Cd = 1.093$ at $\Rey = 4.7\times10^{3}$ to 1.178 at
319: $2.6\times10^{4}$; the 38.1~mm model rises more gently, by about 0.017 per
320: $10^{4}$ in $\Rey$; and the 50.8~mm model shows no trend at all. The overall
321: correlation coefficient between $\Cd$ and $\Rey$ is 0.42. This positive trend is
322: opposite to the classical subcritical behaviour, in which $\Cd$ decreases
323: weakly with Reynolds number up to the critical transition
324: \citep{schlichting2017,zdravkovich1997}. We do not interpret it as a
325: Reynolds-number effect. More plausible explanations are a speed-dependent
326: systematic, such as increased carriage vibration or a small change in model
327: incidence with speed, both of which would raise the apparent mean drag at the
328: higher speeds. Repeat runs at fixed speed, and an independent carriage-speed and
329: vibration measurement, are needed to settle this point.
330: 
331: \subsection{Fluctuating load and vortex shedding}
332: 
333: The force signal at constant speed contains a pronounced periodic component
334: (Fig.~\ref{fig:trace}). The RMS fluctuation is 4.4--6.6\% of the mean drag,
335: with an average of 4.8\%, broadly consistent with reported subcritical force
336: fluctuations \citep{schewe1983,norberg2003}.
337: 
338: The normalised spectra collapse onto a single narrow peak
339: (Fig.~\ref{fig:spectra}). The peak locations give
340: $\mathrm{St} = 0.200 \pm 0.001$ across all 29 runs, with no systematic
341: dependence on diameter or speed. The peak is at $fd/U = 0.40$, i.e.\ twice the
342: expected shedding frequency, as it must be for a streamwise force that has two
343: maxima per shedding cycle. No secondary peaks are visible above the broadband
344: floor, which is roughly 0.2\% of the dynamic force. This is a useful independent
345: check on the experiment: it confirms that the models were shedding in the
346: expected subcritical manner and that the load cell and sampling rate resolved
347: the unsteady loading rather than aliasing it.
348: 
349: \begin{figure}[t]
350:   \centering
351:   \includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{../figures/spectra.pdf}
352:   \caption{Amplitude spectra of the fluctuating drag, normalised by the mean
353:   dynamic force, against dimensionless frequency $fd/U$. All 29 retained runs
354:   collapse onto a peak at $fd/U = 0.40$, corresponding to a Strouhal number of
355:   0.200 for the shedding. The dashed line marks $2\,\mathrm{St} = 0.4$.}
356:   \label{fig:spectra}
357: \end{figure}
358: 
359: \subsection{Blockage and aspect ratio}
360: \label{sec:blockage}
361: 
362: The frontal-area blockage ratio is
363: \begin{equation}
364:   B = \frac{dL}{WH},
365:   \label{eq:blockage}
366: \end{equation}
367: with $W = 0.90$~m and $H = 0.75$~m, giving $B = 2.3\%$, 3.4\% and 4.5\% for the
368: three models. A first-order continuity correction, which assumes that the
369: approach flow is accelerated by the wake displacement and that
370: $U_{\mathrm{local}} = U/(1-B)$, gives
371: \begin{equation}
372:   \Cdc = \Cd\,(1-B)^2.
373:   \label{eq:blockagecorr}
374: \end{equation}
375: The corrected values are listed in Table~\ref{tab:summary} and plotted in
376: Fig.~\ref{fig:cd}b: they fall to 1.055--1.092, i.e.\ 4--9\% below the measured
377: values.
378: 
379: The correction is not applied here, for two reasons. First, Eq.~\eqref{eq:blockagecorr}
380: is a crude bound: it ignores the finite submergence, the free surface, and the
381: fact that the wake is not confined over the full tank depth. Second, and more
382: tellingly, the raw data show no diameter dependence, whereas the correction
383: introduces a 3.5\% spread across the three models. If blockage were the
384: dominant systematic, the measured $\Cd$ would be largest for the 2~in model;
385: it is only 1.2\% larger, which is within the scatter. This suggests either that
386: blockage is weak at these ratios or that it is partly cancelled by
387: aspect-ratio effects: the smallest $L/d$ (2~in) has the strongest end effects,

396: \section{Discussion and limitations}
397: \label{sec:limitations}
398: 
399: Several limitations should be kept in mind when using these data.
400: 
401: \emph{Carriage speed.} The speed is taken from the carriage command and time
402: base. No independent encoder or timing measurement was made, so the speed
403: uncertainty is unknown and is not included in the error bars. Because
404: $\Cd \propto U^{-2}$, this is potentially the largest single source of error in
405: the absolute level. A simple laser or encoder check on the carriage would remove
406: this gap.
407: 
408: \emph{Free surface.} The models penetrate the free surface, and Froude numbers
409: based on diameter, $U/\sqrt{gd}$, reach 2.2 at the highest speed for the
410: smallest model. Wave-making and free-surface deformation are therefore possible
411: at the upper end of the speed range, even though the drag data show no strong
412: speed anomaly that would suggest a large wave-drag contribution. Submerging the
413: models fully, or repeating the tests at several submergences, would separate
414: this effect from the cylinder drag.
415: 
416: \emph{Aspect ratio and end effects.} With $L/d$ between 11.8 and 23.6 the models
417: are finite, and the open lower end and the free-surface intersection both
418: modify the pressure distribution relative to the two-dimensional case. End
419: plates or a splitter plate at the lower end would improve the comparison with
420: two-dimensional data.
421: 
422: \emph{Vibration and alignment.} The positive Reynolds-number trend in
423: Sec.~\ref{sec:results} is the clearest symptom of a speed-dependent systematic.
424: Carriage vibration, model incidence, and load-cell cross-talk all become more
425: important at higher speed and are not quantified here.
426: 
427: \emph{Drift and repeatability.} One run in 30 failed the stationarity check and
428: was rejected. Pre- and post-run tares, and at least duplicate runs at each
429: condition, would make the rejection criterion more robust and would allow the
430: repeatability to be separated from genuine unsteadiness.
431: 
432: \emph{Scope.} Only the streamwise force was measured; lift, pitching moment and
433: wake surveys were not. Turbulence intensity and surface roughness were not
434: characterised. The data set is therefore best regarded as a carefully reduced
435: set of engineering drag measurements, not as a definitive fundamental
436: measurement of the subcritical drag curve.
437: 
438: \section{Conclusions}
439: 
440: Drag coefficients have been measured for three smooth circular cylinders in a
441: tow tank at $4.7\times10^{3} < \Rey < 5.0\times10^{4}$. The main findings are:
442: 
443: \begin{enumerate}
444:   \item The mean drag coefficient is $\Cd = 1.151 \pm 0.030$ across 29 retained
445:   runs, with cylinder means of 1.143, 1.152 and 1.157 for diameters of 25.4,
446:   38.1 and 50.8~mm. The diameter dependence is not resolvable, and the level is
447:   4\% below the classical subcritical value of about 1.2.
448:   \item The run-to-run scatter (3\%) is an order of magnitude larger than the
449:   propagated instrumental uncertainty (below 0.4\%), so the repeatability of the
450:   tow-tank test, not the load cell, limits the precision.
451:   \item The fluctuating drag collapses onto a single spectral peak at
452:   $fd/U = 0.40$, giving a drag-fluctuation Strouhal number of
453:   $0.200 \pm 0.001$. This confirms subcritical vortex shedding and verifies that
454:   the force measurement resolves the unsteady loading.
455:   \item A first-order blockage correction would lower $\Cd$ by 4--9\% but would
456:   introduce a diameter trend that the raw data do not show. Blockage and
457:   aspect-ratio effects are therefore reported as a $\sim$5\% systematic rather
458:   than applied as a correction; resolving them requires a dedicated study.
459:   \item The data set and the complete processing chain are reproducible: the
460:   raw records, calibration files and run log, together with a
461:   \href{https://calkit.org}{Calkit} pipeline that regenerates every processed
462:   table, figure and this PDF, are archived with the paper.
463: \end{enumerate}
464: 
465: Future work should add an independent carriage-speed measurement, repeat runs
466: at each condition, a submergence study to separate free-surface and end
467: effects, and, if possible, a wake survey or companion simulation to quantify
468: blockage.
